newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian ruling party accused of dirty campaign.
newsitem.headline: Romanian ruling party accused of dirty campaign.

text.p: Romanian journalists on Tuesday accused the country's ruling Party of Social Democracy (PDSR) of staging a fake opinion poll aimed at recovering support ahead of parliamentary and presidential elections on November 3.

"Dirty phone calls -- an operation mounted by the PDSR" proclaimed independent newspaper Evenimentul Zilei in a report on how a team of local journalists had uncovered the telephone survey which allegedly aimed to denigrate the PDSR's rivals.

The PDSR retorted that it had commissioned an opinion poll from the "Institute for Public Utilities" (IUP) and accused the political opposition of staging a "commando" operation by breaking into the institute's premises on Monday night.
President Ion Iliescu's spokesman, Traian Chebeleu, declined to comment pending confirmation from "authorised sources."
Romania is the only East European country where former communists retained power after the collapse of the Soviet bloc in 1989.
Latest opinion polls show Iliescu's leftwing PDSR trailing the opposition ahead of next month's elections.
The Association of Romanian Journalists (AZR) accused the PDSR of "dirty electioneering".
"This shows how the authorities are trying to manipulate voters through telephone services," AZR board member Dan Preisz told a news conference at the organisation's headquarters.
A video tape shot by local journalists late on Monday showed panicked workers trying to conceal phone books and questionnaires as reporters entered their offices.

The tape showed youths seated at desks, telephones in hand, triyng to hide from cameras, while an unidentified man apparently in charge shouted: "Cover your books and turn your faces to the wall" when the journalists burst in.

Copies of questionnaires, said to have been used in the survey and made available to the press, included loaded questions about Iliescu's main rivals, academic Emil Constantinescu of the opposition Democratic Convention bloc and Romania's first post-communist prime minister Petre Roman.
"Constantinescu said he would bring ex-King Michael back to the throne if he is elected president. How does that affect your confidence in him?" one question asked.
"If you knew that Roman's wife had asked to be named prime minister in January 1990, on grounds that her husband was unfit for the job, how would your confidence in Roman be affected?" ran another.

The video tape was shot as part of an investigation into the PDSR's campaign run by AZR with help from the December 21 Association, which groups fighters in the December 1989 revolt which ousted Stalinist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.
Responding to the charges, PDSR spokesman Dan Ghibernea told Reuters: "A commando led by members of the December 21 Association broke into the institute last night. Their action is illegal."

But IUP staff denied knowledge of any survey for the PDSR. "Only one opinion survey was commissioned, not by the PDSR, but by a cultural association for elderly people and has nothing to do with the elections," Diana Balan, assistant to the institute's manager, told Reuters by phone.
AZR's Preisz said 200 people had been hired by the PDSR to man phones in offices rented in a building once used by Ceausescu's powerful wife Elena.

The PDSR, which fared poorly in local elections in June, has repeatedly denied accusations by opposition leaders that it was running a dirty campaign for the November polls, which are seen as key for Romania's reform progress.
